title: Insurability Passport Attached to California Home Listings
one_liner: A pre-listing report that verifies wildfire mitigation and attaches bindable insurance options (FAIR Plan plus wraparound, admitted where available) to the listing, so buyers see the real insured cost before they make an offer.
customer: Listing agents and sellers in California wildfire-exposed ZIP codes, paying $149-299 per listing. MGAs and agencies pay commissions on policies that bind from the passport.
problem: Buyers, lenders and agents cannot tell before contract whether a house can be insured or at what price. The FAIR Plan grew to 696,562 policies and $768B of exposure by June 2026 (up 157% since September 2022). Seven of California's twelve largest insurers have stopped writing new business or renewing. Deals slip or die when insurance is discovered in escrow.
solution: A listing add-on that combines a mitigation inspection (Zone 0, vents, roof, photos), an insurability status by carrier type, and indicative premiums for FAIR Plan plus a difference-in-conditions wrap, and admitted quotes where they exist. It also identifies the cheapest mitigation actions that would change eligibility or price. The seller shows a QR code on the listing, and buyers can bind from the passport.
why_now: The California Department of Insurance is pushing the FAIR Plan to offer broader comprehensive coverage (Make It FAIR Act, AB 1680, announced 2026-02-02). Liberty Mutual and Safeco began nonrenewing California condo and renter policies from 2026-01-01. The state also mandates wildfire safety discounts for verified mitigation.
revenue_model: Listing fee of $149-299 for the passport. Commission on bound policies through a partner agency or MGA (typically 10-15% of premium). Optional referral fees from mitigation contractors.
non_obvious_insight: Insurance availability is being handled after the offer, in escrow, although it decides affordability at the moment of offer. Evidence: the FAIR Plan's own key statistics page shows 696,562 policies, $768B exposure and 'fewer coverage options available' in the voluntary market (https://www.cfpnet.com/key-statistics-data/). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_FAIR_Plan lists seven of twelve top insurers pausing new business or renewals. https://www.claimsjournal.com/news/west/2024/12/20/328011.htm shows Safeco and Liberty Mutual leaving condo and renters lines, with nonrenewals beginning 2026-01-01. https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0400-news/0100-press-releases/2026/release005-2026.cfm describes the pending FAIR Plan coverage overhaul. Pre-listing home inspections became a normal seller expense; an insurability passport is the next one, and the mitigation data feeds the moratorium idea above. The main risk is that carrier and FAIR Plan quoting cannot be automated quickly, so start with manual agent-assisted quotes.
first_30_days: Recruit 5 listing agents in Altadena, Sierra Madre, Santa Rosa and Bay Area WUI markets. Partner with one independent agency that quotes FAIR Plan plus DIC. Build a one-page passport (photos, mitigation checklist, three quote scenarios) and deliver it manually for 10 listings at a launch price of $99. Track how many escrows it saves and use those cases to raise the price.

title: Contingency Water-Bill Recovery for Small Commercial Sites
one_liner: A no-win-no-fee service that rebuilds small commercial sites' water, sewer and stormwater bills from the local tariff and claws back irrigation-sewer overcharges, leak credits and stormwater-fee errors.
customer: Owner-operators of small multi-tenant commercial properties (strip centers, 20-200 unit apartment communities, self-storage), churches, private schools and nurseries in cities that bill sewer on metered water and charge stormwater fees. Start in one drought metro. Referral partners are their bookkeepers and property managers.
problem: A $5k-$40k/yr water bill is too small for utility-audit firms, who chase national chains, and too tangled for the bookkeeper, who codes it and pays it. Tariffs sit in council resolutions. Scarcity tiers and surcharges keep changing. Sewer is often billed on metered water that includes landscape water that never reaches the sewer. Stormwater fees rest on impervious-area estimates that are often wrong. Leak-adjustment windows lapse unnoticed. The Fed's 2026 small-business survey names rising costs the #1 financial challenge.
solution: The owner forwards bills or connects QuickBooks/Xero and the utility portal. An LLM pipeline reads the tariff PDF and rebuilds every bill. It flags misclassified meters, irrigation on sewered meters, overnight-flow leak periods in interval data, impervious-area disputes (checked against aerial imagery) and estimated reads. A human analyst files the credit, refund or reclassification with the utility, chases it to cash, and writes corrected coding back into the books. Wedge product: an 'irrigation-sewer plus stormwater credit audit' for one metro and three utilities.
why_now: 49.6% of the US was in drought on Sept 24, 2026 after the warmest June-August on record, so scarcity pricing and surcharges are multiplying. Regulated private water companies invested about $6.8B in 2025 ($43.5B over the decade) and recover it through rate cases that small customers never see. LLMs make it cheap to read hundreds of heterogeneous tariffs and bills. Customer portals increasingly expose interval meter data. Intuit and Xero are rebuilding around LLM subscriptions and cannot easily take contingency fees.
revenue_model: 30% of verified first-year savings plus recovered refunds (contingency). Then a $25/site/month monitoring plan that stops corrections regressing and catches new leak periods. White-label for property managers at about $8/door/year.
non_obvious_insight: The one-time refund is the hook, not the product. The value is the permanent reclassification of the account (meter class, irrigation split, impervious area), which lowers every future bill. The moat is a tariff library that human auditors cannot afford to build for accounts this small. Outcome-priced work does not fit subscription incumbents, so the real competitor is nobody.
first_30_days: Pick one metro with a published stormwater-credit manual and an irrigation or deduct-meter option. Hand-collect five utilities' tariffs. Recruit 20 owners through the local apartment association or BOMA chapter and 5 bookkeepers who get a 10% referral. Audit 24 months of bills per site with the LLM pipeline plus one analyst, with no upfront fee. Targets: 10 audits by day 30, first 3 recovered checks by day 60, then publish anonymized results as the sales asset.

title: Recovery Units: Hospital Step-Down in Lease-Up Apartments
one_liner: Master-lease vacant units in lease-up apartment buildings near hospitals and rent them by the night as staffed 7-30 day recovery apartments for patients who have no safe home to be discharged to.
customer: Hospital care-management and ACO budgets, plus Medicare Advantage and Medicaid plans, pay per diem. Apartment owners get guaranteed rent.
problem: Hospitals hold medically ready patients because home is unsafe, absent or far away. Those avoidable days are commonly cited at $2,500+ each, skilled-nursing beds are scarce, and hospital-at-home programs exclude patients without a suitable home. In the same metros 1.2M apartment units sit in lease-up, with concessions on about 16% of stabilized units (21% in the South, 37% in Austin). Owners of stalled lease-ups need occupancy and real rent, not another free month.
solution: A 10-20 unit block per hospital cluster: furnished, accessible, with home-health nursing and PT visits, meal delivery, a caregiver check-in line and a nurse-led transition plan. Bill a bundled per diem of roughly $175-300 against the $2,500+ hospital day. Owners get a 12-24 month master lease at near face rent with no concession.
why_now: The 2026 lease-up glut and 34-day lease times make owners receptive to any non-haggling tenant. Enhanced ACA subsidies expired and Medicaid work requirements arrive in Jan 2027, so hospitals face rising uncompensated care and margin pressure and are hunting for cheaper post-acute options.
revenue_model: Per-diem revenue minus master-lease and service costs (illustratively $50-80/day margin at 70% occupancy); later capitated arrangements with plans.
non_obvious_insight: A lease-up owner values a tenant that pays full rent on a unit that would otherwise carry a concession, and a hospital values the cheapest safe bed it has ever been offered. The two budgets have never touched because no one operates in between.
first_30_days: Find one lease-up property within 5 miles of a hospital that is running 20%+ concessions. Negotiate 5 units on a 6-month master lease with a 60-day out. Sign a home-health agency. Pitch the hospital's case-management director to trial 10 discharges and invoice per diem in month 2. Check local short-stay rules first and use a 30-day minimum license with early-release credits where needed.

title: Baseline: Bank-Feed Proof of Displacement Costs
one_liner: An app that reconstructs a displaced family's 'normal' spending from pre-loss bank statements and computes the exact increase that Additional Living Expense coverage owes, in carrier-ready format.
customer: Public adjusters and disaster-recovery nonprofits (paying per file), and carriers or TPAs handling long-tail displaced-household claims (paying per active ALE file per month). Consumers use it free.
problem: ALE pays the increase over normal living costs, not the total, so proving it requires a baseline that almost no family has. Adjusters spend hours rebuilding it from memory and shoeboxes, families under-claim (groceries, laundry, mileage, pet boarding, storage, higher utilities) or document sloppily, and disputes turn ugly. With California's new smoke-damage law (AB 1795, effective Jan 1, 2027) barring insurers from cutting off ALE until the home is restored, thousands of standing-home households will run ALE claims for years with heavy documentation demands.
solution: A privacy-first tool that ingests 12 months of pre-loss bank or card data (via open-banking link or uploaded statements), builds a per-category baseline, then diffs it month by month against post-loss spending, matches receipts, and flags gaps the family can legitimately claim (extra mileage, meal delta, rented furniture, storage). Output is an ALE ledger with audit trail in the format desk adjusters actually accept, plus a deadline tracker for policy ALE time limits. Processing is on-device or in a private enclave, and the data is deleted after export.
why_now: More than 13,000 standing-home smoke claims from the Eaton and Palisades fires are still unresolved 20 months later, a lawsuit accuses Farmers' vendor of substandard assessments, and AB 1795 makes ALE duration a live issue. LLM parsing of messy statements and receipts is now cheap and accurate enough to be a product. Carriers are cutting adjusters (entry-level postings down about 50% since 2025) but ALE files still need documentation, so automation that delivers clean files is welcomed.
revenue_model: Public adjusters and recovery groups pay $99-$199 per file. Carriers and TPAs pay $30-$60 per active ALE file per month, or $75-$150 per closed file, in exchange for fewer touches and fewer complaints. Optional referral fees from moving, storage and rental-furniture vendors for legitimate, claimable purchases.
non_obvious_insight: Nobody in the industry records 'normal.' The claim's central number, the increase over normal, is unmeasured on the policyholder's side, and adjusters know most under-claiming is not a coverage denial but the family's inability to prove what they used to spend. Bank data is the only pre-loss record the insured always has.
first_30_days: Build a prototype that categorizes statement CSVs and PDFs into ALE categories and produces a monthly delta ledger. Offer it free to 10 Altadena and Palisades public adjusters and to two survivor-support networks in exchange for feedback and 20 anonymized-consent pilot files. Ask two carrier ALE desk managers to review the output format and sign a paid pilot at $50 per file for 200 files. Prepare a privacy policy and data-deletion promise, because trust is the product.

title: Chip-to-Billet Solid-State Metal Mini-Mills
one_liner: Turn aluminum machining chips directly into billet, rod or wire by friction extrusion, with no remelting, first as a tolling service and then as on-site micro-mills.
customer: Aerospace, defense and precision machine shops with segregated 6061 and 7075 chips, plus extruders and AM wire makers who want recycled content.
problem: Machining chips sell for a fraction of ingot value and are remelted with real melt loss and energy. Aerospace buy-to-fly waste is huge, and domestic aluminum is exposed to tariffs and supply shocks.
solution: Solid-state processing (friction or shear-assisted extrusion, developed at national labs) consolidates single-alloy chips into bar or wire feedstock, preserving alloy chemistry. Phase 1 is a tolling service: ship chips in, get billet back. Phase 2 is a leased on-site mini-mill.
why_now: Tariffs on imported aluminum rose to 50% in mid-2025 and defense and aerospace capacity is stretched. Solid-state processes moved from lab demos toward pilots, so a first product now exists.
revenue_model: Tolling fee per pound returned, then equipment lease plus per-pound fee, plus recycled-content premiums.
non_obvious_insight: Melting destroys the metallurgical history. Chips from a single-alloy shop are effectively pre-alloyed, so solid-state consolidation captures value that a remelt discards.
first_30_days: Partner with a national lab or press builder. Run sample consolidations on chips from 3 shops and test tensile properties. Sell pilot lots to 2 extruders. Apply for AFWERX or SBIR support.

title: Condo Vote Toolkit for Tourist-Flat Bans
one_liner: A compliant e-vote, notice and evidence kit that lets condo communities decide the fate of tourist flats building by building, sold to the property administrators who run those votes.
customer: Property administrators who manage 50-300 buildings each (administradores de fincas in Spain, condominium managers in Brazil) and other managers in cities with short-term-rental limits. Later, mid-term-let operators and hosts who need a 'yes' vote (a firewalled second product).
problem: Tourism regulation is moving from city hall to the building's owners' assembly. Brazil (May 2026) requires 2/3 condo-owner approval, Madrid bans listings without a private entrance, and Barcelona bans all short-term rentals from Nov 2028 (Palma already has a full ban). Spain's 2025 condo-law change also gave owner communities a say over tourist flats (from my knowledge, verify locally). Each vote needs proper notice, quorum, minutes and bylaw amendments. Administrators run this on paper and email, and challenged votes get annulled on procedure.
solution: A per-building workspace with a jurisdiction-specific notice-and-quorum engine, proof of delivery, proxy voting, minutes generation, and local-language bylaw templates approved by local counsel. It adds an incident log (noise, keys, trash) with timestamped evidence and standard letters, plus a 'what is still allowed' guide for converting to compliant mid-term leases.
why_now: Bans and consent rules landing in 2025-2026 force thousands of building-level decisions in the next 12-24 months. Spain's $75M fine on Airbnb (Dec 2025) shows enforcement is real. Stranded short-stay inventory means every owner must choose between a ban and conversion.
revenue_model: About EUR 149 per vote packet, or EUR 2 per unit per month for administrator firms. A separate host-side package (consent-campaign management) at about EUR 500 per approved building, kept firewalled from the neutral tool.
non_obvious_insight: The fight over overtourism has moved to the general assembly of a single building. The buyer who feels the pain is the administrator exposed when a vote is challenged, and no legal-tech vendor sells to these mostly paper-based professionals.
first_30_days: Start with Spain. Build the vote checklist, notice templates and minutes generator in spreadsheets and documents. Offer them to 10 administrators in Barcelona, Madrid and Valencia via the professional-college newsletter at EUR 149 per vote, and aim for 5 paid votes. Automate whichever step they complain about most.

title: Shared Effluent Utility for Depot Industrial Parks
one_liner: A common effluent treatment plant, sold by the gallon, for reshoring tenants at converted military depots and industrial parks.
customer: Redevelopment authorities and economic-development agencies for depots (Anniston, Pine Bluff, Red River, Tooele) and their tenants (magnet and mineral processors, plating shops, battery recyclers). Initial feasibility studies sell for $60-150k.
problem: Critical-mineral processors are taking leases at military depots, and processing generates hard wastewater streams. Permits, not machines, are the bottleneck that drove metal-heavy industry offshore. Each tenant building its own treatment is slow, expensive and a permit risk.
solution: Design, permit and later own and operate a shared pretreatment and zero-liquid-discharge utility with tenant tolling contracts. Begin with a permit-ready 'effluent envelope' study that gives site developers a defensible discharge limit and cost per gallon.
why_now: Federal money of about $2.9B committed to rare earths in June 2026, plus depot leases, plus permit fights over data centers (Cheyenne, Ohio) show water quality as a siting risk. Gradiant's $300M of fab wins prove appetite for industrial reuse.
revenue_model: Study fees, then long-term tolling contracts per gallon treated and a capital recovery charge. Optional public-private financing.
non_obvious_insight: India solved clustered industrial wastewater with common effluent plants decades ago. US reshoring will hit the same wall, and no US firm sells the shared plant as a utility.
first_30_days: Contact the redevelopment authorities at four depots with a $25k 'effluent envelope' scoping offer. Team a process engineer with a permitting lawyer. Line up two tenants' letters of interest to make the first study bankable.

title: Seller-Financing Rails for Paid-Off Homeowners
one_liner: A compliant seller-carry-in-a-box that lets free-and-clear homeowners become the bank, with underwriting, servicing, tax packaging and a note-sale exit.
customer: Retiring owners with paid-off homes and large embedded gains (SF, Chicago and other coastal markets), their listing agents and attorneys, and buyers who cannot or will not take a 7.5% bank loan (self-employed, thin-file, relocating).
problem: 30-year rates are about 7.4-7.6%, 58% more sellers than buyers and 42.5% of listings have price cuts, so deals die on financing. About 40% of owner-occupied homes carry no mortgage, and their owners could earn a better yield than deposits while deferring capital-gains tax through an installment sale. Today seller-carry is a handshake plus a lawyer, with no underwriting, servicing or exit, and federal and state rules on ability-to-repay and balloons make DIY risky.
solution: A packaged workflow: buyer ability-to-repay underwriting, state-specific note and deed-of-trust documents, a licensed sub-servicer with tax and insurance escrow, installment-sale tax packets, and a standing bid to buy the note when the seller wants liquidity. Agents get a listing-side toggle, 'seller-carry available', that widens the buyer pool.
why_now: Record buyer's market with rising rates makes sellers' cheapest concession their own balance sheet. Futures now price a 5% Fed funds rate by end-2027, which makes note yields attractive, and AI document and underwriting tooling makes small-loan servicing economical.
revenue_model: 1-1.5% origination fee paid by the buyer, $25-35 per month servicing, a 1-2 point spread on note sales, and an agent subscription tier.
non_obvious_insight: The best 'rate buydown' is not paying points to a bank but becoming the bank. Free-and-clear boomers hold the largest un-deployed lending balance sheet in housing and are one compliance product away from using it. Sellers with gains above the primary-residence exclusion also get a tax reason to spread proceeds over years.
first_30_days: Choose one state with a workable seller-finance framework and partner with a licensed originator and servicer there. Recruit 30 listing agents from local groups. Sell a $499 flat seller-carry consult to 10 sellers and track how many close. Have counsel sign off on the federal seller-financing exemption conditions before any live deal.

title: Turn Half-Empty School Wings Into Child Care
one_liner: A turnkey operator that leases empty classrooms in half-empty Title I elementary schools and runs licensed infant, toddler and before/after-school care in them.
customer: School districts that lease the space (landlord side). Revenue comes from parents (including those on state child-care subsidies), state pre-K funds, and employers or the district itself buying slots for staff.
problem: Birth-rate decline has left many elementary schools 20 to 40 percent empty, and districts are closing buildings. Yet the neighborhood has no infant care, teachers quit over child care, and before/after-school waitlists run for months. Empty rooms cost the district no visible money, so nobody champions them, and district counsel treats a sublease as a liability risk.
solution: Sell a feasibility and licensing audit ($5k to $15k) covering egress, restrooms, square footage per child, fencing, a separate entrance, and the fire marshal. Then operate the program as a license-holding subtenant. Staff it with cross-trained paras and neighborhood parents. Accept subsidy vouchers and state pre-K slots. Give priority to school staff and Title I families, and keep before- and after-school care in the same building. The district gets rent plus a utilities share, and the operator keeps a thin margin.
why_now: Enrollment declines and school-closure fights are peaking. The 2025 tax law raised the employer child-care tax credit starting in 2026, which helps districts and employers underwrite staff slots. Several states are expanding subsidized or universal child care. Federal after-school funding uncertainty in 2025 also opened a gap for paid programs.
revenue_model: Tuition and subsidy revenue for the operator. One-time feasibility and licensing fees. Optional management fee if a nonprofit or district holds the license.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone talks about reusing closed schools. The money is in schools that stay open but are half-empty, where a wing can be subleased tomorrow with no rezoning. Elementary buildings already meet many child-care code items: kid-height restrooms, exits, a playground and a kitchen. The principal knows this from living in the building. The blocker is the district's lease template and its fear of liability, and both are solvable with paperwork.
first_30_days: Map licensing rules in one state and find a nonprofit child-care operator willing to hold the license. Pitch 5 superintendents and principals with a two-page space-utilization audit and a sample lease. Sell three $5k feasibility audits to fund the pilot, and use waitlists from existing before/after-school programs as proof of demand.

title: Certification-Ready OS for Sober Living Operators
one_liner: Software and audit-readiness for independent recovery residences, so the good operators become visible, certified and eligible for opioid-settlement and referral funding.
customer: Independent sober living and recovery residence operators (8-40 beds), who pay a monthly subscription. Counties, states and treatment programs later pay for verified-quality dashboards.
problem: Sober living is a largely informal industry with a few notorious bad actors. States are moving to certification, and funding streams increasingly require it. Good small operators run on spreadsheets and can't prove house rules, incident handling, naloxone logs, drug-testing policies and fair-housing compliance. Funders and hospital discharge planners can't tell who is real.
solution: A recovery-residence operating system built around the NARR standard and each state's certification rules. It covers rent and bed management, house-rule acknowledgments, incident and naloxone logs, drug-test policy records, complaint handling and resident outcomes. It has a gap assessment and mock certification audit, and generates an audit binder. A separate funder dashboard reports verified occupancy and quality metrics.
why_now: Ohio made certification mandatory in January 2025, and Virginia followed in July 2025. New York launched its first recovery residence certification program in early 2025. Certification has become a gatekeeper for state opioid-response subawards, opioid-settlement contracts and Medicaid reimbursement in some states. The SUPPORT reauthorization signed December 1, 2025 extended HUD's Recovery Housing Program and SAMHSA grants through FY2030.
revenue_model: $199-499 per house per month for the operating system. $1,500-3,000 certification-prep packages. Annual license fees from counties, health plans or opioid-settlement administrators for verified-bed and quality dashboards. Do not take pay-per-referral fees: federal and state patient-brokering laws (such as EKRA) make that dangerous.
non_obvious_insight: The gray market's problem is invisibility as much as bad operators: funders have no cheap way to tell good houses from bad. The trusted data trail is the product. The business model rule is to sell software to operators and dashboards to funders, and never take referral commissions. That keeps the network legally clean and trusted by courts, hospitals and families, which is what makes it hard to copy.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a new certification mandate (Ohio or Virginia). Offer 10 operators a free gap assessment against the NARR standard through state recovery-housing associations. Convert them to a $199/month readiness plan. Meet the state certifying body to align templates. Pitch one county opioid-settlement administrator on a pilot verified-bed dashboard.

title: Airline-Grade Depot Maintenance for Drone Fleets
one_liner: A swap-based depot and records service that applies airline maintenance discipline to police drone-as-first-responder, ag-spray and utility inspection fleets.
customer: Sheriff's offices and municipal police and fire departments running 5-30 docked drones, agricultural spray operators, and utility and rail inspection contractors. The buyer is the program manager or operations lead, paying per airframe per month.
problem: Drone programs are run by one enthusiastic officer or a few pilots. Flying is the easy part. The real risks are battery cycle counts and swelling, motor and prop wear, firmware drift across a fleet, undocumented crash repairs, and no clear rule for when an aircraft is airworthy enough to dispatch. Aircraft techs recognize all of it: life-limited parts, configuration control, intermittent faults, 'no fault found', and sign-off traceability. Agencies also need records that survive scrutiny in court or after an incident. Manufacturer service plans cover their own hardware only and are mostly warranty repair, not fleet discipline.
solution: A monthly airframe subscription that includes a rotable-style exchange pool. When something fails, we ship an airworthy replacement airframe, gimbal or battery set overnight and take the broken one to our bench, so the program is never down. We keep per-airframe and per-battery records with QR codes, cycle counts and firmware baselines. We run a pre-deployment inspection checklist that acts like a simple minimum-equipment list for dispatch. Records are exported in evidentiary format. Techs staffing the bench are retired or moonlighting A&Ps.
why_now: The 2025 White House drone executive order and the FAA's proposed BVLOS rule (Part 108) point toward large fleets flying beyond visual line of sight, and hundreds of US police and fire departments are standing up drone-as-first-responder programs. Tightening US restrictions on Chinese-made drone equipment mean installed fleets must be kept flying for years while spare parts get scarce, which makes maintenance skill a moat. Mechanic supply is also loosening at the edges as retired A&Ps look for part-time work.
revenue_model: $450-900 per airframe per month for the exchange and records subscription, fixed-fee inspections ($150 per airframe), battery-audit fees, parts margin on refurbished airframes, and later a training and certification product for agency pilots.
non_obvious_insight: Drone programs will relearn every airline lesson, and the money is in configuration control and records, not in flying. A rotable exchange pool beats field repair because the customer's real pain is downtime and liability, not the repair cost. Manufacturers mostly sell to fleets of one brand, but real fleets are multi-vendor, so an independent depot with an airline-style record system has room to win.
first_30_days: Pick one metro and sign three agencies or ag operators to a discounted pilot at $450 per airframe per month. Set up a bench in a rented hangar bay or garage with two part-time A&Ps. Run the record system on Airtable with QR labels, and sell battery-health audits and pre-deployment inspections at fixed prices as the first paid products. Use an airline-style monthly 'fleet status' report as the marketing piece. By day 30, the target is at least one signed agreement and a small exchange pool of two spare airframes.

title: AI Provenance Audits for Game IP Deals
one_liner: Due-diligence audits, plus a signed process-capture plugin, that tell publishers and acquirers what in a game is verifiably human-made and what IP they actually own.
customer: Small and mid publishers, game aggregators and acquirers, and lenders (idea 1's future competitors). Festival and award organizers pay for finalist verification. They pay $1.5-6k per audit. Studios and freelance artists pay $0-199 for the evidence pack.
problem: Steam's AI disclosure is self-attested. In January 2026 the form was narrowed to player-facing generative content. About one in five store listings now disclose AI use, and players punish undisclosed use, including refund fights over late disclosure. The US Copyright Office position is that purely AI-generated material isn't copyrightable, so a publisher buying a game with heavy AI art owns thinner IP than the price assumes. Awards bodies have reversed honors after discovering AI use.
solution: Two parts. First, a local plugin set (Aseprite, Krita, Blender, Photoshop, plus git and Perforce hooks, and C2PA where available) writes a tamper-evident, timestamped hash chain of authoring events, with no screen recording. Second, an audit desk takes a shipped build and repo and produces an asset-by-asset provenance map: evidenced human, AI-assisted, or unknown. It adds a Steam-disclosure recommendation and a copyrightability memo prepared with counsel.
why_now: Valve's January 2026 form rewrite left studios unsure what counts. AI use is now mainstream (roughly 20% of listings) and controversial. Awards and festivals are getting burned. Publishers are adding AI warranties to contracts and want a way to verify them.
revenue_model: Per-audit fees, bulk pricing for publishers with catalogs, a per-finalist fee for festivals and awards, and a paid studio subscription for evidence-pack export. Artists get the credential free, which builds the network.
non_obvious_insight: Classifiers run on shipped assets are unreliable, and false positives on human artists are reputational poison. The only defensible evidence is process metadata captured at creation, which is nearly impossible to reconstruct afterward. So the buyer is the balance-sheet buyer who cares about IP ownership, not the player. Freelancers who want a 'verified human' credential to win commissions pull the tool into studios from below.
first_30_days: Hand-sell audits: contact 30 small publishers and aggregators, and do 3 discounted audits by reading source-control history and interviewing the team. Ship a minimal Aseprite or Krita plus git capture plugin. Pitch two indie festivals or awards on verifying their finalists. Publish an anonymized 'what audits usually find' write-up.

title: Legal Hold and Discovery for Agent Traces
one_liner: Custodian mapping, hold notices and defensible export for the agent logs that are becoming the new email in litigation.
customer: Litigation-support teams at mid-size law firms and corporate legal-ops or GC teams at companies running agents, with boutique e-discovery providers as a channel.
problem: Agent traces (prompts, tool calls, retrievals, memory) sit in observability tools and vendor consoles with retention defaults of days to weeks. They are not on custodian charts, and at least one court has treated AI-generated content as discoverable, exposing parties to Rule 37(e) spoliation sanctions. EDRM and law-firm alerts in mid-2026 say agent logs become evidence when agents fail, but nobody sells the plumbing.
solution: Connectors to Langfuse, LangSmith, OpenTelemetry and S3 stores, agent platform APIs and cloud logs. They inventory where traces live, generate agent custodian maps, flag legal holds and suspend deletion where APIs allow, snapshot with hash chains, redact PII and privileged material, and export to Relativity, Everlaw or Reveal. Add hold-aware deletion to reconcile GDPR erasure requests with active holds, and a Rule 26(f) checklist.
why_now: Agents moved into production across 2026, and the discovery literature has just started addressing agent traces. Observability vendors optimized for developer debugging (short retention, cheap storage), which is the opposite of what litigation needs.
revenue_model: $2-10k per matter plus $1-3k/month per connected source, with revenue share for e-discovery channel partners.
non_obvious_insight: E-discovery vendors will need new data sources the way they needed Slack and Teams connectors. Whoever owns the connectors to agent trace stores becomes the toll gate, and forensics tools that reconstruct incidents are not litigation-grade preservation.
first_30_days: Build 3 connectors (Langfuse, LangSmith, OpenTelemetry/S3) and a one-page hold notice and agent custodian questionnaire. Recruit 3 boutique litigation-support firms as pilots and sell a $5k agent ESI readiness assessment to GCs.

title: AI Re-Post Radar with First-Publication Proof
one_liner: A seal-then-watch tool that timestamps a creator's work before publishing and finds AI-reworded, re-voiced copies, with a ready-to-file complaint.
customer: Educational and commentary YouTubers, podcast producers and paid-newsletter writers with 10k-500k audiences, and small MCNs that manage them.
problem: The industry argues about whether a piece is AI-made. For a creator being ripped off, the deciding fact is who published first. Faceless channels can transcribe, reword and re-voice a human video or post within hours. YouTube's Jul 16 policy on generic or repetitive content helps in principle, but enforcement depends on complaints, and long-tail creators lack Content ID-style tooling.
solution: A pre-publish 'seal' takes a hash of script, audio and footage plus an embedding of the transcript, anchored to a public timestamp log. A radar then checks YouTube, TikTok, Substack, Medium, RSS and podcast directories for semantic near-duplicates, using transcript embeddings so reworded copies still match. It scores them, and drafts a YouTube reused-content complaint, DMCA notice or EU DSA notice with the timestamp proof attached.
why_now: Rewriting and re-voicing are now nearly free, while platforms have just adopted policies that penalize repetitive content but rely on rights-holders to report. Embeddings make cheap semantic matching practical.
revenue_model: $29-99/month per creator, $5 per auto-filed takedown bundle, and agency plans for MCNs.
non_obvious_insight: Origin time beats origin type. A timestamped record survives rewording, re-encoding and watermark stripping, while 'made by AI or not' is a probabilistic argument. The evidence is the product.
first_30_days: Build a transcript-and-embedding pipeline on the YouTube Data API and Whisper, limited to each customer's niche keywords. Recruit 10 creators from YouTuber Discords and demo by finding real re-posts of their videos within the first hour. Charge $29/month after the free scan.

title: Funeral Committee Escrow and Fixed-Price Vendor Network
one_liner: A per-funeral M-Pesa vault where contributions can only be released to pre-priced vendors with two-of-three committee approvals, ending the 'where did the burial money go' fights.
customer: The family and burial committee (treasurer, chair, village elder, workplace welfare group) organising a rural funeral, usually with a Nairobi or diaspora fundraising arm. Vendors (tent and chair hire, caterers, coffin makers, embalmers, hearse and PA operators) are the second paying side.
problem: A rural funeral is often a family's biggest single cash event, drawing hundreds of mourners and costing multiples of a year's farm income. It is run on WhatsApp groups and an exercise book. Treasurer fraud and 'the money vanished' accusations are common and can split families for years. Vendors quote inflated prices to grieving families who cannot shop around, mortuary storage fees accrue daily so decisions are rushed, and families often sell land, borrow against coop shares or take mobile loans to close the gap. Existing crowdfunding tools collect money but do nothing about how it is spent.
solution: Each funeral gets a dynamic M-Pesa paybill account and a WhatsApp bot (English, Swahili, Sheng). The committee picks from fixed-price packages (basic, standard, large) with vendor prices published. Every payout to a vendor till needs two of three designated approvers by USSD PIN, and a live ledger is visible to all contributors. The bot also handles pledge tracking, reminders in the Nairobi and home committees, the mortuary and transport schedule, and a post-funeral accounting statement. Money sits in a licensed payment provider's trust account, not on the startup's balance sheet.
why_now: M-Pesa paybill, till and B2B payout APIs are mature enough to make programmable escrow cheap, and the WhatsApp Business API is inexpensive. LLMs now let a bot handle Swahili and Sheng committee chatter. The post-2023 cost-of-living squeeze makes families more sensitive to funeral overspending and to selling land to pay for it. Funeral crowdfunding has trained diaspora and urban Kenyans to give online, but nobody controls the spend side.
revenue_model: About 2-3% fee on money flowing through the vault plus negotiated vendor margins or referral commissions of roughly 8-12% on vendor spend. Later upsells are funeral cover (partnered with a licensed insurer), memorial pages, and body-transport routing between Nairobi and up-country.
non_obvious_insight: Money that is locked to named vendors is welcome, not resented: it protects the treasurer from the 'sharing tax' of relatives and neighbours asking for cash, and from accusations. In effect the product sells social protection, not payments. Funerals are also where families mortgage their long-term farm assets, so reducing funeral overspend is a farm-resilience product that VCs would never classify as agtech.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 vendors (tents, catering, coffins, hearse) along one corridor such as Nairobi to Murang'a or Nyeri and agree fixed package prices. Onboard the first 5 funerals by offering free setup through church welfare groups, alumni groups and your own contacts, using a manual approval flow on top of an existing paybill provider. Charge the fee only after a funeral closes with a clean statement, and use those statements as proof for the next 50.

title: Court-Rules MCP Server With a Deadline Warranty
one_liner: Effective-dated, human-verified court rules, judge standing orders and deadline math for one state at a time, exposed to any AI agent, with fee credits if a computed deadline is wrong.
customer: Solo and small firms (5 or fewer attorneys) in personal injury, family, criminal defense and landlord-tenant who already run Clio or MyCase and are starting to use Claude or ChatGPT agents. Later, legal-AI vendors that buy the rule set by API.
problem: Missed deadlines are among the most common malpractice claims (background knowledge, verify). General models know case law roughly but not this county's local rules, this judge's standing order (including AI-use certifications), or this year's fee schedule. The rules live as PDFs across thousands of court sites and change constantly, and big-firm docketing systems are priced and built for large firms.
solution: Start with one state pack, for example Texas civil. It holds statutes of limitation, civil procedure, local rules of the top counties and judge standing orders, each effective-dated with a hashed source PDF. MCP tools such as compute_deadline(event, court, date) and check_filing(court, judge, doc_type) return the date, the rule cites and a confidence flag. A deterministic engine does the date math (no LLM arithmetic), paid legal editors verify the high-use rules, and change alerts go out. A small warranty (fee credit plus capped reimbursement) backs the deadline output.
why_now: 8am's MyCase says 60+ firms, mostly 5 or fewer attorneys, adopted its Claude MCP connector (73 actions) in the first month, so small firms are now consuming practice tools through agents. Case law is open and the model is free, but local procedure is not in any frontier legal product.
revenue_model: $79-149/month per firm per state pack, an API license of $2-10k/month for legal-AI vendors, and a premium warranty tier.
non_obvious_insight: When the model is free and the corpus is open, the scarce asset is authoritative, effective-dated local procedure with a liability wrapper. Nobody can warrant an LLM's legal reasoning, but a rules engine plus editorial verification is exactly where a warranty is underwritable.
first_30_days: Pick one state and one practice area. Hand-build the 300 highest-frequency rules with two contract paralegals (about $8-10k), ship a free MCP server, and recruit 15 firms through a state solo and small-firm bar list. Charge $99/month after the trial, publish an accuracy audit, and keep the warranty to a $500 credit until loss data exists.

title: Farm Income Dial: ACA Cliff Management
one_liner: A December planning service that uses the grain-contract and input-prepay levers farmers already control to keep household income under the 400% poverty cliff and avoid repaying a full year of health subsidies.
customer: Farm families who buy ACA marketplace coverage. KFF estimates about 27% of farmers do, nearly triple the adult average. The co-op grain desks and rural CPA firms that advise them pay for a white-label version.
problem: The enhanced ACA subsidies expired on December 31, 2025, so the hard cutoff at 400% of poverty is back (roughly $130k for a family of four). The 2025 tax law also removed repayment caps for tax year 2026. A farm family that projected income under the line and then lands $2,000 over must repay every dollar of advance credits, often $15k to $25k. Farm income is lumpy and depends on prices and yields nobody knows in January. Farm CPAs optimize the federal tax bracket, not the ACA cliff, and nobody connects the two.
solution: Farmers connect their grain settlements, deferred contracts, prepaid inputs and equipment purchases. The tool tracks estimated 2026 MAGI against the cliff and gives a concrete action list: how many bushels to defer into 2027, how much fertilizer to prepay, when to elect CCC loan treatment, when to buy equipment. It also models plan choice for 2027 open enrollment, including Farm Bureau non-ACA plans and their underwriting risks. Every recommendation is reviewed by the household's CPA, so this is planning software and not tax advice.
why_now: This is the first tax year with no repayment cap and no enhanced credits. Marketplace enrollment fell from 22.1M to 19.2M in a year. The planning window closes December 31, 2026, and every Iowa farm family on a marketplace plan is exposed right now.
revenue_model: $350 to $600 per farm household per season. Broker commissions from carriers when the tool places 2027 coverage. White-label licenses to rural CPA firms and co-op grain desks ($50 to $100 per client). Optional success fee of 10% of the protected credit.
non_obvious_insight: The ACA cliff is controlled with the same pen that signs deferred-payment contracts. The co-op grain desk is the real MAGI control panel for farm families. CPAs do not see it because they only meet clients in February, after the levers are gone.
first_30_days: Partner with 2 rural CPA firms and one co-op grain desk. Build a spreadsheet-grade calculator plus a one-page 'cliff letter' for clients. Run a 'Cliff Night' at the co-op with farm families in October and November. Convert 30 to 50 households at $350 before the December deadline and document dollars saved.

title: Storm-Chaser Livestreams as Claims Evidence
one_liner: License the timestamped, geotagged archives of storm-chaser channels as address-level date-of-loss evidence for hail, wind and flood claims.
customer: Public adjusters, policyholder attorneys and roofing-claim desks in hail states (Colorado, Texas, Nebraska, Minnesota) first. Parametric hail and wind MGAs and appraisal umpires second.
problem: Hail claims turn on whether hail of a given size hit an address on a given date. Radar estimates are error-prone at swath edges, and spotter reports are sparse. Hail drives 26-54% of Colorado premiums (secondary source). Colorado's HB25-1182 (in force since July 2026) and California's AB 75 give owners disclosure and appeal rights, but the evidence burden stays on them ('owners still have to prove their case'). Meanwhile storm chasers stream thousands of hours with GPS, timestamps and hailstones held next to coins, and that ground truth sits unmonetized on YouTube.
solution: Sign revenue-share licenses with chaser channels. Index their archives by time, location and hail size, using computer vision on reference objects, and pair each clip with radar. Sell a 'Date-of-Loss Dossier' per address: nearest verified clips, size estimate, uncertainty and chain of custody. Distribute a printed reference 'hail card' standard to chasers. Add a 'go verify' request queue where adjusters or parametric carriers post bounties on active storms and fans can top them up by tipping.
why_now: Storm-chase livestreaming is now a fan-funded media business with huge live audiences. New state laws create disputes that need evidence. Parametric MGAs need data that cuts basis risk. The 2025-26 hail seasons are still inside claim windows, and the spring 2027 season is six months away, so the archive-first version can sell now.
revenue_model: $39-149 per dossier from public adjusters and roofers, $2-5K a month API access for MGAs and claims shops, and 40-50% revenue share to creators.
non_obvious_insight: The densest hail sensor network in America is a fandom already paid for by fans. Insurers' problem is not data volume but admissible, attributable data, and chasers go exactly to the worst cell. Ground truth is a by-product of entertainment, so the sensor cost is already covered.
first_30_days: Approach 15 mid-size chaser channels (10K-300K subscribers) with a rev-share license for their 2024-26 archives. Index 200 hail events. Sell the first 50 dossiers to 5 Colorado and Texas public adjusters and roofing claim reps for open claims. Draft the reference-card standard for the spring 2027 season.

title: Trade-Crew Capacity Forward Book for Builders
one_liner: A 12-week forward view of subcontractor crew availability for regional homebuilders, giving small builders the trade-partner visibility that Lennar has in-house.
customer: Regional builders and general contractors doing 50-800 homes a year in Texas, Florida and the Southeast, which pay a monthly subscription. Framing, drywall, landscape, paving and electrical subs join free.
problem: Labor availability is turning into a constraint in specific trades and regions. Lennar says roughly 20% of its divisions are under greater pressure from localized immigration enforcement and data-center construction, and crews vanished with little notice (landscaping was the example). Paychex reports its blue-collar clients cannot find electricians. Small builders can't see 3-4 months ahead the way Lennar's purchasing teams do, so a crew that disappears becomes a delayed closing.
solution: A weekly text or WhatsApp pulse asks each sub for crew size, planned availability by week, licensing and insurance status, and a lawful-workforce attestation such as E-Verify participation. The data rolls up to a builder dashboard showing committed versus needed crew-days by trade and community, with alerts when a sub's committed capacity drops. A shared bench lets builders pool vetted backup crews in the same metro, with a per-placement fee. The pitch is schedule continuity. Compliance data is a by-product.
why_now: Enforcement and the data-center construction boom are hitting trade labor at the same time as builders' closing cycle times are at record lows (116 days at Lennar). Builders are compressing schedules just as crews get less predictable. Starts are down, which gives builders leverage today but makes them dependent on retaining subs when volume returns.
revenue_model: $400-$1,500/month per builder division, plus a $150-$400 fee per successful backup-crew placement, plus a paid insurance-and-attestation verification tier for subs.
non_obvious_insight: The winner's edge at scale is information, not labor supply. Lennar's Jim Parker says purchasing teams 'have tremendous visibility with our partners' and can 'allocate their crews to where we need them', with 3-4 months of crew visibility, while Stuart Miller says 'labor availability has started to become more of an issue', citing 'localized immigration enforcement and data center construction' and landscaping crews as the example (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/17/lennar-len-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). Paychex's CEO says clients 'are having trouble finding people ... a need for a lot of electricians and construction work' (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/24/paychex-payx-q1-2027-earnings-call-transcript/). KB Home sees no labor problem today, so the risk is regional and uneven (https://www.fool.com/earnings/call-transcripts/2026/09/23/kb-home-kbh-q3-2026-earnings-call-transcript/). A large builder's advantage is a relationship graph, which small builders can rebuild cheaply with a weekly text poll. It should be pitched around schedule continuity.
first_30_days: Pick one metro (for example DFW or Tampa) and one trade (landscape or framing). Recruit 3 regional builders and 25-40 subs via builder purchasing managers. Run the weekly text pulse manually with a shared Google Sheet and Twilio, and deliver a Monday capacity report by email. Charge $500/month from week 4 on a 90-day pilot. Vet legal language on workforce attestations with an employment lawyer before launch.

title: Protein Allocation Co-op for Mid-Size Brands
one_liner: A buyers' co-op that pools forward volume for whey and reformulates around shortages for brands too small to get allocation.
customer: Mid-size sports-nutrition, RTD beverage and bar brands (roughly $20-200M revenue) that lack direct cheese-plant relationships.
problem: Whey isolate is around $14/lb, some suppliers are sold out through 2026, and big buyers lock allocations, so small brands pay spot prices or get nothing.
solution: Aggregate members' forward demand into direct contracts with mid-size cheese and whey processors, and run a reformulation desk that blends whey with alternative proteins to spec.
why_now: The constraint is downstream whey-processing capacity and cheese output rather than raw milk, and factories are retooling for cottage cheese, so relationships and volume commitments now decide who gets protein.
revenue_model: Annual membership plus a 2-4% margin on pooled volume and fees for the reformulation desk.
non_obvious_insight: The shortage is partly a market-structure problem for small buyers rather than an absolute supply problem. Aggregation turns a set of unattractive small accounts into one large, plannable contract.
first_30_days: Recruit 8-10 brands into a founding cohort with combined tonnage, then hold calls with five mid-size cheese and whey plants to test whether they will commit capacity to a pooled buyer.

title: The Junior Bench: Rent-a-Resident for AI Review
one_liner: Mid-size accounting, legal and insurance firms rent trained new grads for 12 weeks to verify their AI-produced work, rebuilding the vanished junior rung as a paid residency.
customer: Regional accounting firms, boutique law firms, insurance brokerages and healthcare revenue-cycle companies; new grads join as paid residents.
problem: Employers stopped hiring juniors because AI does the grunt work, yet they still need future seniors. AI-exposed majors have 5 points lower initial employment, grads are 42% underemployed, and 22-25 year-olds in exposed jobs are 19% below trend. Meanwhile firms carry liability for AI-drafted work that nobody is trained to verify well.
solution: A cohort residency. Two weeks of domain and AI-verification training, then about ten weeks embedded in the firm's workflow reviewing AI-drafted workpapers, contract abstracts or claims against sources, with seeded-error scoring. The firm pays a weekly rate and can convert residents to hires. Each resident builds a scored 'verification record' that becomes the credential.
why_now: Payroll data show a widening hiring gap since August 2025. Firms are AI-first but facing quality and liability incidents, and partner pipelines will look empty in about five years.
revenue_model: About $1,800-2,500 per resident-week from the firm against roughly $900-1,100 wage cost, giving 40-50% gross margin. Optional conversion fee if hired early.
non_obvious_insight: AI did not remove the junior job; it turned it from doing into checking. Checking is a trainable, measurable skill with an obvious buyer: the firm that carries the liability for AI errors.
first_30_days: Sell to 3 regional CPA firms ahead of busy season with 5 residents each. Recruit from local accounting grads. Build an error-injection test set to score residents. Charge from week one.

title: Fifteen-Minute Court Reporting for Family Law Hearings
one_liner: Remove the half-day minimum by dispatching remote stenographers into many short hearings per day, so a family-law litigant gets a certified record of a 15-minute hearing for about $100.
customer: California family law and probate attorneys and solo practitioners. Self-represented litigants reached through DV legal aid organizations and family law facilitators. Legal aid groups buying bulk credits. Later, county courts contracting to meet the new duty to provide records to indigent litigants.
problem: California logged roughly 3 million civil, family and probate hearings without a verbatim record between April 2023 and March 2026, about 7 in 10. Without a record, appeals of custody and restraining-order rulings fail, because the appellant cannot show error. Private reporters charge $250-$500+ appearance minimums, since a reporter can wait 2-3 hours for a 12-minute calendar item. Nobody pays that for a routine hearing. In 2026 the California Supreme Court (Family Violence Appellate Project v. Superior Court) held that courts must give indigent litigants an official verbatim record on request, and courts do not have the reporters to comply.
solution: A dispatch platform that reads court calendars, predicts when each matter will be called from historical hearing-type durations per department, and pages a remote reporter into the court's Zoom or Teams feed only for the minutes needed. One reporter covers 8-12 short hearings a day across departments. Deliver a certified transcript in 24-72 hours, with an AI first draft for the reporter to scope. Price is a flat $95 for hearings up to 15 minutes and about $8 per page beyond that. Start where remote appearance and remote reporting are allowed (California's AB 3013 authorizes remote reporting, and each court's procedures need checking). Pitch courts on per-department-day capacity at a discount to staffing a full-time reporter.
why_now: The 2026 California Supreme Court ruling creates a legal duty courts cannot currently meet. AB 3013 (2024) opened remote reporting. The workforce is projected to be about 5,500 reporters short by 2030. Family courts are widely on video. Reporter dead time is a scheduling problem that software can solve.
revenue_model: Per-hearing fees paid by attorneys and litigants. Bulk credits funded by legal aid and foundation grants. Later B2G contracts priced per courtroom-day. The reporter keeps about 55-60% of each hearing fee, which beats their typical hourly yield because dead time is eliminated.
non_obvious_insight: The reporter shortage is partly a utilization problem. In a busy family calendar department, a reporter may write 2-3 hours of a 7-hour day and wait the rest. Remote hopping sells that dead time to several litigants at once, so the price can fall 70% while the reporter earns more.
first_30_days: Sign 3-5 remote-capable freelance or semi-retired reporters. Pick one county whose family departments run on Zoom and cover it manually with a shared spreadsheet and a text pager. Offer 10 solo family law attorneys and two DV appellate nonprofits (start with the Family Violence Appellate Project) at-cost coverage of their next 5 hearings. Track wait time per hearing so the prediction model has real data.

title: Orphan-Element Audits for Copper Concentrate and Tailings
one_liner: A 90-day survey that measures the tellurium, selenium, bismuth, cobalt, germanium, rhenium, indium and scandium copper mines already ship for free, then brokers by-product credit rights with refiners.
customer: Mid-size copper miners (Arizona, Utah, Nevada, Chile, Peru, Zambia, Kazakhstan) who sell concentrate to smelters or run SX-EW, paying $40-120k per site survey. Refiners and specialty-metal buyers (Aurubis-type smelters, Umicore, 5N Plus-type processors) pay finder fees. Government programmes such as DoD DPA Title III and DLA support recovery projects.
problem: Smelter contracts pay for Cu, Au and Ag. Te, Se, Bi, Co, Ge, In, Sb and Re are either given away, or shown only as penalty elements (As, Sb, Bi, Hg, F). The plant lab measures the penalty elements and stops. The 48-element ICP-MS suite exists only on exploration drill core from ten years ago and never on the concentrate, tailings, SX raffinate or electrolyte bleed streams. The smelter quietly captures value in anode slimes and flue dust. The miner has no data to negotiate with. Meanwhile, benchmark treatment charges for 2026 reportedly collapsed to around zero, so smelters are squeezed and newly hunting for by-product margin and for clean feed. Chinese export controls on Te, Bi, In, Ga, Ge, Sb and others make Western buyers desperate.
solution: A productised survey: pull 30-60 retained samples from process streams (every mine keeps monthly composite retains), run multi-element ICP-MS plus automated mineralogy through partner labs, and deliver an 'orphan-element balance' showing tonnes per year and contained value per element. Then hand the mine a negotiation kit: by-product participation clauses for offtake contracts, dust and slime credit language, and penalty-threshold renegotiation. Route the data to refiners and toll processors who can recover the element. The compensation is a survey fee plus 10-20% of by-product margin for 5 years, or a finder fee at contract signing.
why_now: In 2025 China imposed export controls on tellurium, bismuth, indium, gallium, germanium and antimony, with rare earths restrictions following. US and EU strategic stockpile, offtake and grant programmes now pay for domestic by-product supply. Smelters are under profit pressure from near-zero treatment charges and are open to sharing upside with suppliers. Prices for Te and Bi jumped.
revenue_model: $40-120k per site survey, plus a 10-20% by-product royalty or finder fee on recovered element revenue, plus a refiner-side subscription for a pipeline of quantified feed.
non_obvious_insight: The barrier is not technology. Kennecott has produced tellurium for decades. It is that nobody measured, so nobody owns the value, and contracts were signed when no one cared. The person who knows how the process streams flow (where it goes to anode slimes, where to dust) can tell which stream concentrates each element.
first_30_days: Ask ten friendly mid-tier mines for retained composite samples, or buy access to public tailings and concentrate assays. Run 15 multi-element packs at $60-150 each (about $2k in total). Produce a one-page 'value at stake' per mine and email it to 30 operations and commercial managers. Sell 2-3 pilot surveys at $25k. Meanwhile call two refiners and one federal programme office with the resulting map to line up demand.

title: Compliance-as-Code for EWA and BNPL
one_liner: State-by-state earned wage access and BNPL rules are being written fast. Turn them into an API that checks fees, tips and disclosures before each product release.
customer: EWA and BNPL providers, payroll platforms and neobanks adding these features, and employers running EWA programs.
problem: Colorado sued EarnIn (2026-09-08), Maryland banned EWA tipping, and New York and Illinois have BNPL rules. Each state differs on fees, tips, disclosures and licensing. Product managers ship copy and fee configs faster than lawyers can review them.
solution: A rules engine and configuration API. Providers submit product configs (fees, tip prompts, speed, limits) and get per-state pass/fail, required disclosure text, and a change log. It also monitors new bills and enforcement actions and produces exam-ready evidence.
why_now: Enforcement began in Sept 2026 and legislatures are still moving. Providers need pre-release checks now and will need audit trails when examiners arrive.
revenue_model: $3k-$10k per month per provider, with per-state add-ons and content licensing to law firms.
non_obvious_insight: EWA's legal risk sits in UI copy and fee configuration, which product teams change weekly. Rules-as-code plugs into release management, which a law-firm memo never can.
first_30_days: Publish a free 12-state EWA and BNPL rule tracker as a lead magnet. Pair with a fintech law firm and pitch five mid-size providers and payroll platforms on a $3k per month pilot.

title: Indigenous-Language Voice Compliance for Farm Crews
one_liner: A WhatsApp voice assistant that delivers heat-safety training and piece-rate confirmations in Mam, K'iche', Mixtec and Triqui.
customer: Growers and farm labor contractors with mixed-language crews, especially in CA, WA and OR.
problem: Many farmworkers speak indigenous languages rather than Spanish, so heat-illness training, piece-rate records and pay disputes break down and audit trails are weak.
solution: Voice-first check-ins, safety micro-trainings, piece-rate ticket confirmations and dispute logs using recent multilingual speech models, with native-speaker review and audit-ready records.
why_now: Speech models released in 2025 cover far more low-resource languages, and crew turnover and enforcement pressure raise the cost of compliance failures.
revenue_model: $3-6 per worker per season or a per-crew monthly fee, sold to growers and contractors.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance vendors serve English and Spanish, so the workers at highest risk have the weakest record. Language coverage is the product.
first_30_days: Partner with two contractors, recruit native-speaker reviewers, and pilot heat-safety check-ins with one crew.
